title: Starting Plants

learn.summary: Starting from seed costs pennies per plant and unlocks hundreds of varieties garden centers never carry. Most vegetable seeds germinate best in 65-75°F soil; tomatoes and peppers like 70-85°F. The classic beginner mistake is starting too early — count back from your last frost date (6-8 weeks for tomatoes) instead of sowing in January.

do: Sow one 6-cell tray of a fast, easy crop (lettuce or basil) indoors this week and record the sow date and days to sprout

children.title: Seed Starting Setup

learn.summary: Use sterile seed-starting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and carries damping-off fungus. Sow at a depth of 2-3 times the seed's diameter; surface-sow tiny seeds like lettuce that need light. Bottom-water by setting cells in a tray of water so the surface stays undisturbed and fungus is discouraged.

do: Bottom-water your seed tray every time this week: 15 minutes sitting in an inch of water, then drain — never sprinkle from above

children.title: Germination

learn.summary: Germination needs the right combination of moisture, temperature, and sometimes light — warmth matters most, and a $20 heat mat can cut pepper germination from 3 weeks to 7 days. Test old seed with a wet paper towel in a zip bag: 10 seeds, one week, count sprouts for your germination percentage. Most veggie seed stays viable 2-5 years stored cool and dry.

do: Run a paper-towel germination test on your oldest seed packet: 10 seeds, damp towel, zip bag on top of the fridge, count sprouts in 7 days

children.title: Light for Seedlings

learn.summary: A windowsill is almost never enough — seedlings stretch into leggy, weak stems reaching for light. Give 14-16 hours a day under an ordinary LED shop light hung 2-4 inches above the leaves, raised as plants grow. A $10 outlet timer makes this automatic.

do: Hang a shop light on adjustable chains 3 inches above your seedlings and set a timer for 16 hours on, 8 off

children.title: Propagation from Cuttings

learn.summary: Many plants clone readily from a 4-6 inch stem cutting: strip the lower leaves, and root in water (pothos, basil, mint, coleus) or in moist mix, often helped by rooting hormone (rosemary, hydrangea, figs). Roots appear in 1-4 weeks. Softwood cuttings taken in late spring root fastest.

do: Take a 4-inch basil or mint cutting today, strip the bottom leaves, and root it in a glass of water on the windowsill — pot it up when roots hit one inch
